title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1LC0LE_---1LD_1LE1LB_1RA0LF_0RD1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1LC0LE_---1LD_1LE1LB_1RA0LF_0RD1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is a sequence of linear phases: in each, the head bounces at the left end and moves one word w = 1111110 from a block into a run of 1s (or builds w's out of a run), at constant rates; seen to 3·109 steps. Lean proves the eight shift rules across the words. Halting needs B to read 0 with a 0 on its left; where a phase ends and the next begins is where that could happen, and the map from one phase to the next was not derived.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Shift rules across the words
claims.text: E and A run right across blocks of w = 1111110 and x = 111110 (rewriting their rotations), and B, C, D, E run left across rotations of w.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: Only C reading 0 halts; C is entered only from B reading 0 (1LC), so the machine halts exactly when B reads a 0 that has a 0 on its left (0 B> 0). Read off the table.

claims.title: Linear phases
claims.text: Sampled with the head in A at the left end: in a drain phase w x wa 0 0 1b R becomes w x wa−1 0 0 1b+15 R every 3 visits (the tape grows by 8 cells); in a build phase w x wa 1111 0 wc 0 0 1b R becomes w x wa+2 1111 0 wc−3 0 0 1b+15 R. E.g. w103 0 0 1424 at step 2,001,556, w102 0 0 1439 at 2,016,698, w101 0 0 1454 at 2,031,696. Observed in the run, not proved.

claims.title: No halt to 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps; the registers
claims.text: At step 1,366,620,342 the tape (55,573 cells) reads 1 04 x2 w19 14 0 14 0 w2279 02 111707 w x w2311 02 111514 w2 19 w2 02 15: three blocks of w and two runs of 1s.
claims.where: a word-view run of the tape (the tokrun view of tools/c)

claims.title: No closed tape language with small windows
claims.text: bbtools.ctl K = 3..6 leaves halting configurations; n-gram CPS widths 3 to 7 fails; no invariant a·ones + b·pos + W mod 2..12.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 41,072 cells have been visited and 36,943 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.535). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The phases are linear and the halting pattern 0 B> 0 could only come at a change of phase; the map from one phase's end to the next phase's start (a Collatz-like map on the register values, presumably) was not derived.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB1RD_1LC0RF_1LD0LB_1RE0RB_---1RA_0LA1RC up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 41,072 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Blocks of 7-cell words and long runs of 1s
html:
Write w for the seven cells 1111110 and x for 111110. At step 2,001,556 the tape (1,843 cells) is

[A1] 1 0 0 w x w^103 0 0 1^424 w^2 x^105 0 0 1^2 w x^2 0 0 1^10

The head is at the left end. The tape is a few registers: blocks wa and runs 1b separated by 0 0. The left part grows (like a square root of time); the far right end hardly moves.

sections.heading: Draining one register into another
html: Every three visits to the left end, one w leaves the block and the run of 1s gains 15: w103 0 0 1424 at step 2,001,556, w102 0 0 1439 at 2,016,698, w101 0 0 1454 at 2,031,696. When the block is empty a different phase starts: one block grows by 2 and another shrinks by 3 per round, while a run of 1s grows by 15. The head crosses the words with the shift rules proved in Lean (A and E going right, B, C, D, E going left).

This is the behavior of a small register machine: linear phases, each one emptying a register, and a change of phase whose outcome depends on the values left over. Later the tape holds more registers, e.g. at step 1,366,620,342: ... w2279 0 0 111707 w x w2311 0 0 111514 ....

sections.heading: Only on 0 B> 0
html: The machine stops only when C reads a 0, and C is reached only from B reading 0 and stepping left. So it stops exactly when B reads a 0 next to another 0. Inside the phases the head never does that; the question is what happens at the changes of phase, where the leftover register values decide the next phase. That map was not derived, so the question is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.535). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051).
After 109 steps the tape spans 41,072 cells (33,101 left of the start, 184 right), with a density of 1s of 0.899.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB1RD_1LC0RF_1LD0LB_1RE0RB_---1RA_0LA1RC: rename A→C, B→D, C→E, D→A, E→B, F→F and exchange left and right; it is this table started in state D, in a mirror

summary: A register machine on the tape: blocks of 7-cell words w = 1111110 and long runs of 1s, which phases of bounces at the left end drain one into the other at fixed rates (one w becomes fifteen 1s), with new registers appearing as the tape grows.
